chapters.title: Teach and Disciple
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, teaching is pointing the way, and a disciple is someone who learns by living with the teacher
chapters.trueMeaning: Learning a way of life by following
chapters.nutshell: We often think of teaching as passing on information and of a disciple as a church member. In Hebrew, to teach (*limmed*) is to make someone learn, and *torah* means “instruction” that points the way. A *talmid* (in Greek *mathētēs*) was a student who lived with a teacher, copied his life and carried on his way.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical teaching aims at a changed life, and a disciple is an apprentice who follows a teacher so closely that he becomes like him.
skeleton: We usually think of teaching as lessons and information
Lamad / limmed: learning and teaching come from one root
Yarah and torah: teaching means pointing the way
Shanan: impress God's words on your children, at home and on the road
Talmid and rabbi: the student lives with the teacher
Greek didaskō and mathētēs carry the same picture
Jesus' great commission is to make disciples, not only converts
Discipleship is imitation, done together, for all of life

p: When we hear the word **teach**, most of us picture a classroom: a teacher at the front, students taking notes, and an exam at the end. Teaching means passing on information, and learning means remembering it. In church the word **disciple** often just means “a Christian” or someone who attends a course for new believers.

The Bible's words point to something much bigger. In Hebrew and in the Greek of the New Testament, teaching is about **a way of life**. A teacher shows the road, and a disciple walks it beside him. The goal is not only that you know more but that you become more like the one you follow.

sections.h: Lamad: to learn and to teach
p: The basic Hebrew verb is *lamad* (לָמַד), “to learn”. In another verb form, *limmed* (לִמֵּד), the same root means “to teach”, that is, literally “to cause someone to learn”. So in Hebrew, teaching is measured by whether the other person actually learns.

Moses tells Israel: “Hear, Israel, the statutes and the rules… and **learn** them and be careful to do them” (Deuteronomy 5:1). God gathers the people at Sinai “that they may **learn** to fear me… and that they may **teach** their children” (Deuteronomy 4:10). Learning here is never only head knowledge; it ends in fearing God and doing what he says. The psalmist prays, “Blessed are you, O LORD; **teach** me your statutes!” (Psalm 119:12).

From the same root comes *talmid* (תַּלְמִיד), “student”. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, “teacher as well as pupil” (1 Chronicles 25:8), but it became the everyday word for a disciple in later Jewish writing. Another word from the root is *Talmud* (תַּלְמוּד), “study, learning”, the name of the great body of rabbinic teaching.

sections.h: Yarah and torah: teaching that points the way
p: A second verb is *yarah* (יָרָה). In its simplest form it can mean “to throw” or “to shoot” an arrow. In the causative form, *horah* (הוֹרָה), it means **to instruct, to show, to point the way**. God says to Moses, “I will be with your mouth and **teach** you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:12). From the same root comes *moreh* (מוֹרֶה), “teacher” (Isaiah 30:20).

Most famous of all is *torah* (תּוֹרָה). We usually translate it “law”, but its basic meaning is **instruction** or **teaching**. God gives Moses the stone tablets “with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction” (Exodus 24:12). A father says to his son, “My son, do not forget my **torah**” (Proverbs 3:1), and he clearly means his loving teaching, not a legal code.
> Torah is not first a rulebook. It is a loving parent or teacher pointing and saying, “This is the way. Walk in it.”

sections.h: Shanan and hevin: teach diligently, make people understand
p: In the Shema, Israel's central prayer, God says: “These words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall **teach them diligently** to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).

The verb is *shanan* (שָׁנַן). Its basic meaning is “to sharpen”, so it pictures **impressing** God's words sharply on a child's mind. Jewish tradition also connects this teaching with repetition, and a related root, *shanah* (שָׁנָה) “to repeat”, gives the name *Mishnah*, the first great collection of rabbinic teaching learned by repeating it aloud.

Notice where this teaching happens: at home, on the road, at bedtime and in the morning. In the Bible the first classroom is **the family**, and the lesson is taught by everyday life as much as by words.

After the exile, Ezra “had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to **teach** his statutes and rules in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). The order matters: study, then do, then teach. A teacher must first live what he teaches.

When Ezra read the Torah to the people in Jerusalem, the Levites “**helped the people to understand** the Law… They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:7–8). The verb here is *hevin* (הֵבִין), “to make someone understand”. Biblical teaching is not just reading words aloud; it is explaining them until people grasp them.

sections.h: The Greek words: teacher, teaching, disciple
p: The New Testament uses *didaskō* (διδάσκω), “to teach”. Jesus “opened his mouth and **taught** them” (Matthew 5:2), and the crowds were amazed “for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew 7:28–29). A teacher is a *didaskalos* (διδάσκαλος). John explains the Hebrew title for his Greek readers: “Rabbi (which means **Teacher**)” (John 1:38). *Rabbi* (רַבִּי) literally means “my master” or “my great one”.

What a teacher gives is *didachē* (διδαχή), “teaching” (Mark 1:22, 27). The first believers “devoted themselves to the **apostles' teaching** and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42), and an early Christian handbook was simply called *the Didache*, “the Teaching”.

A disciple is a *mathētēs* (μαθητής), from a verb meaning “to learn”. It is the Greek match for the Hebrew *talmid*: **a learner who follows a teacher**. Jesus says, “A disciple is not above his teacher… It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher” (Matthew 10:24–25). The aim of being a disciple is likeness.

When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they usually rendered *torah* with *nomos* (νόμος), the ordinary Greek word for “law” or “custom”. That was a natural choice, because the Torah does contain commandments and civil laws.

But over time, in Western ears, “the Law” came to sound cold and legal, the opposite of grace. The Hebrew word is warmer and wider. It includes stories, songs, promises and wisdom, all of it **God's instruction** for a good life. When the psalmist says, “Oh how I love your law!” (Psalm 119:97), he is delighting in his Teacher's guidance, not in a list of penalties.

sections.h: Disciples in the Jewish world of Jesus
p: In Jesus' day, Jewish teachers gathered students who left home to live with them. The Mishnah's collection of the sayings of the sages begins with the advice: “raise up many disciples” (Mishnah Avot 1:1). Another early sage said, “Let your house be a meeting place for the sages; **sit in the dust of their feet**, and drink in their words thirstily” (Mishnah Avot 1:4). The picture is of students so close to the teacher that they are covered with the dust he raises as he walks.

A disciple learned not only the teacher's words but his whole way of life: how he prayed, ate, kept the Sabbath and treated people. Jewish tradition also spoke of taking on “the yoke of the Torah” (Mishnah Avot 3:5). In that setting Jesus says: “Take my **yoke** upon you, and **learn from me**, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He is inviting people to become his students and to take up his way of living.

So when the risen Jesus says, “Go therefore and **make disciples** of all nations… teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20), the verb is *mathēteuō* (μαθητεύω), “make disciples”. The goal is not just decisions or converts but **apprentices** who learn to live as he lived.

sections.h: Western habits vs the Jewish lens
p: A common Western habit is to treat faith as a set of correct ideas, so teaching becomes the transfer of doctrine and discipleship becomes a short course. The biblical picture is more like an apprenticeship: you walk with someone wiser, you watch, you imitate, and you are corrected along the way.

This does not make knowledge unimportant. Ezra studied, the Levites explained, and Jesus taught with authority. But in the Bible, learning that does not change how you live has not yet reached its goal. Paul could say, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), because teaching was meant to be seen as well as heard.

To be a disciple today is to stay close to Jesus through Scripture, prayer and the company of his people, and to let his way shape ordinary life. Ask not only “What do I know?” but also “Whom am I becoming like?”

And every disciple is meant to help others learn. Parents teach at the table and on the road, older believers walk with younger ones, and friends read Scripture together. Teaching in the Bible's sense is something all of us can do: **live the way, and invite others to walk it with you**.

chapters.title: Witness and Apostle
chapters.subtitle: A witness tells what they have seen, and a sent one carries the sender's message and authority
chapters.trueMeaning: Living evidence, sent with the King's authority
chapters.nutshell: We often think of “witnessing” as a sales pitch for Jesus. In Hebrew, an *ed* is a witness in a courtroom who tells what they have seen, and Isaiah pictures Israel as God's living evidence before the nations. A *shaliach* or *apostolos* is a “sent one” who carries the sender's message and authority.
chapters.bigIdea: God's people are witnesses whose words and lives give evidence of what God has done, sent out by Jesus as he was sent by the Father.
skeleton: We often think of witnessing as a technique or a pitch
Ed: a witness in court tells what they saw and heard
Isaiah 43: God calls Israel his witnesses before the nations
Edut: the tablets of testimony kept in the ark
Shalach and shaliach: the sent one carries the sender's authority
Greek martys and apostolos carry the same pictures
A witness gives evidence with a life, even at great cost
We are sent as Jesus was sent

p: For many Christians, **witnessing** means a method: a conversation script, a tract, a set of steps to lead someone to a decision. It can feel like selling a product, and many of us feel guilty because we are not good at it.

The Bible's words come from a different world: the **courtroom** and the **royal messenger**. A witness is someone who has seen and heard something and tells the truth about it. An apostle is someone who is sent by another with his message and authority. Both pictures are about faithfulness to what is true and to the one who sends us, not about clever technique.

The Hebrew word for a witness is *ed* (עֵד). In Israel's law a person could not be condemned on one person's word: “Only on the evidence of **two witnesses or of three witnesses** shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15). A witness had to be honest, because a false witness could destroy an innocent life, and the ninth commandment forbids it (Exodus 20:16).

A witness can also be a thing that stands as evidence. Jacob and Laban set up a heap of stones and said, “This heap is a **witness** between you and me today” (Genesis 31:48). Joshua told the people who promised to serve the LORD, “You are witnesses against yourselves” (Joshua 24:22). A witness, then, is **living or visible evidence** that something is true.

In Isaiah 43–44, God sets up a great courtroom scene. The nations are called to bring witnesses for their idols: “Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right” (Isaiah 43:9). But the idols have no witnesses, because they have done nothing.

Then God turns to Israel: “**You are my witnesses**,” declares the LORD, “and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (Isaiah 43:10). And again: “You are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me?” (Isaiah 44:8; see also 43:12).

Israel's role was not to win an argument but to **be the evidence**. Their history of rescue from Egypt, their life under God's teaching and their worship of the one God were meant to show the nations who God is.
> A witness does not invent the story. A witness tells what God has done, and the witness's own life is part of the evidence.

From the same root comes *edut* (עֵדוּת), “testimony”. God told Moses, “You shall put into the ark **the testimony** that I shall give you” (Exodus 25:16). The stone tablets of the covenant are called “the testimony”, and the ark is called “the ark of the testimony” (Exodus 25:22).

The tablets were a lasting witness to the covenant: a record of what God had said and what Israel had promised. At the heart of Israel's worship stood **a testimony**, God's own word kept among his people as evidence of his relationship with them.

sections.h: Shalach and shaliach: the one who is sent
p: The Hebrew verb *shalach* (שָׁלַח) means “to send”. In Isaiah's vision God asks, “**Whom shall I send**, and who will go for us?” and Isaiah answers, “Here I am! Send me” (Isaiah 6:8). God sends prophets, messengers and deliverers throughout the Bible.

In rabbinic Hebrew, a person sent to act for someone else is called a *shaliach* (שָׁלִיחַ), an agent or “sent one”. The Mishnah states a famous rule: “**A person's agent is like the person himself**” (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). A shaliach could sign a contract, deliver a message or even arrange a betrothal on behalf of the sender, and what he did counted as the sender's act. The person who leads prayer in the synagogue is still called the *shaliach tzibbur*, “the sent one of the congregation”.
So a sent one does not speak for himself. He carries **the sender's message and authority**, and how people treat him is how they treat the sender.

sections.h: The Greek words: martys and apostolos
p: The Greek word for witness is *martys* (μάρτυς). The Greek translation of Isaiah 43:10 uses it: “Be my witnesses.” After the resurrection Jesus tells his followers, “You are **witnesses** of these things” (Luke 24:48), and “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Related words are *martyria* and *martyrion* (μαρτυρία, μαρτύριον), “testimony” (John 1:7; Acts 4:33), and the verb *martyreō* (μαρτυρέω), “to testify”: “The Spirit of truth… will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 15:26–27).

Because so many witnesses to Jesus were killed for their testimony, the word slowly took on a new meaning. Jesus speaks of “Antipas my faithful witness, who was killed among you” (Revelation 2:13). By the second century, *martys* was used for someone who died for the faith, which is where the English word **martyr** comes from.

An *apostolos* (ἀπόστολος) is “one who is sent”, from the verb *apostellō* (ἀποστέλλω), “to send”. Jesus chose twelve “so that they might be with him and he might **send them out** to preach” (Mark 3:14). Many scholars see the apostle as close to the Jewish idea of the shaliach, though they debate how direct the link is. Jesus himself says, “a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger (*apostolos*) greater than the one who sent him” (John 13:16). Hebrews even calls Jesus “the **apostle** and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1): he is the Father's own Sent One.

In John's Gospel, Jesus often speaks of himself as the one the Father **sent**. Then he passes that mission on: “As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world” (John 17:18). After the resurrection he says, “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). (In this verse John uses *apostellō* for the Father's sending and another common verb, *pempō*, for Jesus' sending; both mean “send”.)

This is the shaliach idea at full strength. Jesus' followers carry his message and act in his name. The apostles said, “We cannot but speak of **what we have seen and heard**” (Acts 4:20), and John writes, “That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes… and touched with our hands… we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us” (1 John 1:1–3).

sections.h: Western habits vs the Jewish lens
p: When witnessing is treated as a sales technique, success is measured by how persuasive we are and how many people respond. In the Bible's picture, a witness is measured by **faithfulness**: telling the truth about what God has done and living in a way that agrees with it.

This takes pressure off and adds responsibility at the same time. We do not have to win every argument; the Spirit is the main witness (John 15:26). But our lives are part of the evidence. Peter tells believers to be ready to give a reason for their hope, yet “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15), and to live so well that others see their good deeds (1 Peter 2:12).
Being a witness starts with **seeing and hearing**: spending time with Jesus in Scripture, prayer and community, and noticing what God is doing. You can only tell what you have actually seen.

Then it means speaking honestly and living consistently, at home, at work and among your neighbours. You are a sent one, carrying the King's message of good news and acting in his name. And like Israel in Isaiah's courtroom, your shared life with God's people is itself evidence that **the LORD is God and there is no other**.

In Isaiah 43–44 God calls Israel his witnesses, living evidence before the nations that he alone is God.
The covenant tablets were called “the testimony” (edut), kept in the ark at the heart of worship.
A shaliach is a sent one: “a person's agent is like the person himself” (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5).
Greek martys means witness; because many witnesses died for their testimony, it later gave us “martyr”.
An apostolos is one sent with authority; Hebrews calls Jesus himself “the apostle”.
Witness is faithfulness in word and life, not a sales technique; the Spirit is the main witness.
